name: Data Analytics
tagline: SQL plus a dashboard tool plus one real project — a genuinely reachable path.
description: Data analysts answer business questions with data: pull it with SQL, clean it, visualize it, and explain what it means to people who don't read spreadsheets. It is one of the more accessible no-degree paths because the skills are demonstrable — a portfolio of real analyses substitutes convincingly for credentials — and because analyst work exists in every industry, including the retail and logistics ones you may already know.

salaryRange.note: Entry-level data/business analyst range in most US markets. Analyst titles vary wildly — 'reporting analyst' and 'operations analyst' often pay similarly and are less competitive than 'data analyst'.

remoteFriendly.note: Analysis work is laptop work and remotes well. Entry-level analyst roles are somewhat less remote than senior ones, and hybrid is common.

realityCheck: 'Data analyst' postings attract enormous application volume, much of it from career changers with the same Google certificate. The certificate alone will not distinguish you. Two or three real analyses of messy public data — with your conclusions and your reasoning written out — will.
whyItFits: Retail and warehouse work is full of data nobody analyzes: shrink, staffing versus footfall, pick rates, delivery windows. If you can do an analysis of a business you already understand, you have a portfolio project with genuine domain insight, which is rarer than technical skill.

motivation.quote: The analyst who understands the business beats the analyst who only understands the tools. You already understand a business.
motivation.story: A repeated pattern: someone working retail builds a dashboard analyzing their own store's staffing against sales volume, shows it to their district manager, and gets moved into an internal reporting role — no external job search at all. Internal moves into analytics are common because the company already trusts you and you already know what the numbers mean.
motivation.source: Composite of the pattern described in r/analytics and r/BusinessIntelligence career threads

interviewPrep.question: Write a query showing total sales per region, only for regions with more than $100K in sales.
interviewPrep.why: Tests GROUP BY plus HAVING — the single most common SQL interview trap. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?
interviewPrep.why: Asked in essentially every analyst interview. Explain with a concrete example of when rows would be lost with INNER.

interviewPrep.question: Sales dropped 20% last month. How would you investigate?
interviewPrep.why: The most important question in the interview and it isn't technical. Segment it: which products, which regions, which channels, which customer types? Compare against seasonality and last year. Check whether the data pipeline broke before assuming the business did.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between correlation and causation, and why does it matter here?
interviewPrep.why: They want evidence you won't hand leadership a misleading chart. Have a real example ready.

interviewPrep.question: How do you decide which chart type to use?
interviewPrep.why: Comparison across categories: bar. Change over time: line. Part-to-whole: usually still a bar, not a pie. Relationship: scatter. Saying 'and I'd ask who's reading it and what decision it supports' scores well.

interviewPrep.question: You find duplicate rows in a dataset. What do you do?
interviewPrep.why: Determine why they're there before deleting anything — duplicates are often a join problem in your own query rather than a source data problem. Then document the decision.

interviewPrep.question: How would you explain your analysis to someone non-technical?
interviewPrep.why: This is most of the job. Lead with the answer and the recommended action, then the supporting evidence, then caveats — never the methodology first.

steps.title: Get genuinely good at spreadsheets
steps.description: Excel and Google Sheets are still the most-used analysis tools in the world, and many analyst jobs are 60% spreadsheet work. Learn pivot tables, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, conditional formatting, text functions, and charting. Google Sheets is free and works on a phone or library computer, so this whole step costs nothing.
steps.costNote: Free. Google Sheets requires no purchase and covers everything at this stage.
steps.outcome: You can build a pivot-table-driven summary of a messy dataset without help.
steps.resumeBullet: Advanced spreadsheet skills: pivot tables, lookup functions, data cleaning, and dashboard-style reporting in Excel and Google Sheets.

resources.name: Excel Easy (free tutorials)
resources.notes: Free, well-structured, no signup.

resources.name: Google Sheets training (free, official)
resources.notes: Free official training. Sheets is free to use with any Google account.

resources.name: ExcelIsFun (free YouTube channel)
resources.notes: Free. Thousands of videos including full multi-hour courses.

steps.title: Learn SQL until it's comfortable
steps.description: SQL is the non-negotiable skill of this path — it appears in nearly every analyst job posting and is tested live in most interviews. Get to the point where SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, CTEs, and window functions are all familiar. Several excellent SQL tutorials run entirely in the browser, so a library computer is enough.
steps.costNote: Free. SQLBolt, Mode's SQL Tutorial, and Select Star SQL are all free and browser-based.
steps.outcome: You can answer a business question by writing a multi-table query with aggregation.
steps.resumeBullet: Proficient in SQL: multi-table joins, aggregation, subqueries, CTEs, and window functions for business reporting and analysis.

resources.name: SQLBolt (free interactive lessons)
resources.notes: Free, browser-based, no signup. The best zero-friction starting point.

resources.name: Mode SQL Tutorial
resources.notes: Free. Teaches SQL through real analytical questions rather than syntax drills.

resources.name: Select Star SQL
resources.notes: Free interactive book working through one real dataset in depth.

resources.name: DataLemur / StrataScratch SQL interview questions
resources.notes: Free tier of real analyst interview questions; paid tiers optional.

steps.title: Complete a structured analytics certificate
steps.description: The Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate is the recognized entry credential here. It will not by itself get you hired, but it gives structure, a portfolio capstone, and a line on the resume that HR filters recognize. Coursera's financial aid application is approved routinely — apply for it rather than paying if money is tight.
steps.costNote: PAID: $49/month on Coursera — roughly $150 if you finish in three months, $294 if it takes six. Apply for Coursera Financial Aid first; it can reduce this to $0 and approval is common.
steps.outcome: Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate completed.
steps.resumeBullet: Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate — data cleaning, SQL, R, Tableau, and end-to-end analysis of a real dataset.

resources.name: Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate (Coursera)
resources.notes: PAID: $49/month subscription. Financial aid available — apply and wait about two weeks for a decision.

resources.name: Coursera Financial Aid application
resources.notes: Free to apply. Routinely approved for professional certificates; this is the honest way to do the certificate at no cost.

resources.name: Microsoft Power BI Data Analyst (PL-300) — alternative credential
resources.notes: PAID, $165. More technical and more respected in Microsoft-shop job markets. Free learning path on Microsoft Learn.

steps.title: Learn a BI/visualization tool
steps.description: Power BI or Tableau — pick based on local job listings, though Power BI has broader enterprise adoption and Power BI Desktop is free on Windows. Learn to connect to data, model relationships between tables, write basic DAX or calculated fields, and build a dashboard someone could actually make a decision from.
steps.costNote: Free: Power BI Desktop is a free Windows download, and Tableau Public is free. Only publishing/sharing in the paid services costs money, which you don't need for learning.
steps.outcome: A dashboard you built from raw data that answers a specific question.
steps.resumeBullet: Built interactive dashboards in Power BI/Tableau: data modeling, calculated measures, and visualizations designed around specific business questions.

resources.name: Power BI Desktop (free download)
resources.notes: Free on Windows. The full authoring experience costs nothing.

resources.name: Microsoft Learn — Power BI training paths
resources.notes: Free official training.

resources.name: Tableau Public (free)
resources.notes: Free. Doubles as portfolio hosting — your published vizzes have shareable public URLs.

resources.name: Workout Wednesday (free weekly viz challenges)
resources.notes: Free weekly challenges in Tableau and Power BI. Excellent portfolio fuel.

steps.title: Learn Python for data (pandas)
steps.description: Not every analyst job requires Python, but it raises your ceiling and separates you from the certificate-only crowd. Learn pandas for loading, cleaning, joining, and aggregating data, plus basic plotting. You do not need software-engineering depth — you need to be able to clean a messy CSV that would defeat a spreadsheet.
steps.costNote: Free. Kaggle Learn and Google Colab run in a browser — no installation, works on a library computer.
steps.outcome: You can clean and analyze a 100,000-row messy dataset in a notebook.
steps.resumeBullet: Analyzed and cleaned large datasets with Python and pandas, including merging multiple sources, handling missing data, and producing visual summaries.

resources.name: Kaggle Learn — Python and pandas micro-courses
resources.notes: Free, browser-based, short. The most efficient free path to working pandas skills.

resources.name: Google Colab (free notebooks in the browser)
resources.notes: Free. No install needed, which makes Python accessible without owning a PC.

resources.name: Python for Data Analysis (Wes McKinney, free online edition)
resources.notes: Free online. Written by the creator of pandas.

steps.title: Build two or three real portfolio analyses
steps.description: This is the step that gets interviews. Take messy public data — or better, data from an industry you actually know — ask a specific question, answer it, and write up the finding for a non-technical reader. Structure each writeup as: question, data source, what you had to clean, what you found, what you'd recommend, what the limitations are. The last section is what makes you look like an analyst instead of a student.
steps.costNote: Free. Public data, free tools, free hosting.
steps.outcome: Two or three published analyses with clear findings and recommendations.
steps.resumeBullet: Published end-to-end data analyses using public datasets: defined the question, cleaned and joined multiple sources in SQL/Python, visualized results, and delivered written recommendations with stated limitations.

resources.name: data.gov (US open data)
resources.notes: Free. Large, genuinely messy real-world datasets — messiness is a feature here.

resources.name: Kaggle Datasets
resources.notes: Free. Convenient, though heavily used — differentiate through your question, not your dataset.

resources.name: Maven Analytics Data Playground
resources.notes: Free curated datasets built for portfolio projects.

resources.name: Tableau Public / GitHub Pages for hosting writeups
resources.notes: Free portfolio hosting with shareable links you can put on a resume.

steps.title: Analyze something at your current job
steps.description: The highest-leverage move available to you: pick a real question at your current workplace, answer it with the data you already have access to, and show it to a manager. Staffing versus sales by hour, shrink patterns by category, delivery exception rates. Worst case it's a great portfolio piece; best case it turns into an internal transfer, which is the single most common way retail workers become analysts.
steps.costNote: Free. Check your employer's data policies first — use only data you're authorized to see, and never take company data home.
steps.outcome: An analysis a real manager read and responded to.
steps.resumeBullet: Identified an operational inefficiency by analyzing internal performance data and presented findings and recommendations to management.

resources.name: Storytelling with Data (blog, free)
resources.notes: Free articles on presenting analysis to non-technical audiences — the skill that gets analysts promoted.

steps.title: Apply broadly across analyst titles
steps.description: Do not search only 'data analyst.' Reporting analyst, operations analyst, business analyst, inventory analyst, marketing analyst, and revenue analyst are often the same job with less competition. Applying to roles in an industry you already know — retail, logistics, warehousing — is a real advantage that most applicants can't claim.

resources.name: Indeed — data analyst listings
resources.notes: Free. Search the adjacent titles separately — they surface substantially different results.

resources.name: r/analytics
resources.notes: Free. Realistic discussion of the entry-level analyst market.

resources.name: BLS Occupational Outlook — data and operations research analysts
resources.notes: Free. Official US wage and outlook data — use it to sanity-check salary claims you see online.
